content: Cervical cerclage is a surgical procedure performed during pregnancy, where a suture is placed around the cervix to provide mechanical support and reduce the risk of preterm birth. Despite its widespread use, the safety and effectiveness of this intervention remain subjects of debate. This review aimed to evaluate whether cervical cerclage improves pregnancy outcomes in women with singleton pregnancies who are at high risk of pregnancy loss due to factors such as a history of preterm birth, a short cervix identified on ultrasound, or findings from a physical examination. The review included 15 randomized controlled trials involving 3,490 women, with three additional trials (152 women) added since the last update in 2012. The studies compared cervical cerclage to either no treatment or alternative interventions. The evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach to determine the quality of the findings. When comparing cerclage to no cerclage, the procedure likely reduces the risk of perinatal death, although the confidence interval includes the possibility of no effect (relative risk [RR] 0.82, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.65 to 1.04; moderate-quality evidence). However, when stillbirths and neonatal deaths were analyzed separately, the data were less reliable due to smaller sample sizes and fewer events. For stillbirths, the RR was 0.89 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.75; low-quality evidence), and for neonatal deaths before discharge, the RR was 0.85 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.39; low-quality evidence). Serious neonatal morbidity did not differ significantly between women who received cerclage and those who did not (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.18; low-quality evidence). Similarly, the likelihood of delivering a baby who was discharged home healthy was comparable between the two groups (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.06; moderate-quality evidence). Cervical cerclage was associated with a reduced risk of preterm birth before 37, 34, and 28 weeks of gestation. For preterm birth before 34 weeks, the average RR was 0.77 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.89; high-quality evidence). Subgroup analyses based on clinical indications (e.g., history-indicated cerclage, short cervix identified on ultrasound, or physical exam-indicated cerclage) did not provide sufficient data to draw meaningful conclusions, and no evidence of differential effects was observed. Two trials (129 women) compared cerclage to vaginal progesterone in women with a short cervix identified on ultrasound. These trials were too small to detect reliable differences in outcomes. Another trial compared cerclage to intramuscular progesterone (75 women) but also lacked the statistical power to identify significant differences between groups. Evidence from two trials (344 women) comparing history-indicated cerclage to ultrasound-indicated cerclage was insufficient to determine differences in clinically important outcomes. In conclusion, cervical cerclage reduces the risk of preterm birth in women at high risk of preterm delivery and likely reduces the risk of perinatal death. However, there is no evidence to suggest that the effectiveness of cerclage varies based on clinical indications such as obstetric history or short cervix. The comparative effectiveness of cerclage versus other preventive treatments, particularly vaginal progesterone, remains uncertain due to limited data.
